title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Marcus Chen
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture-and-standards guidelines covering API design, coding standards, infrastructure (IaC and networking), model-serving best practices, observability requirements, performance targets and benchmarking, and the Decision Record (ADR) process. It is intended as the canonical starting point for engineers designing or reviewing new services, model integrations, and infra changes.

Principles

- Production-first: designs must prioritize reliability, predictable latency, and operational clarity.
- Observable by design: any new service or model integration must emit defined metrics, traces, and structured logs.
- Reproducible infra: all infra changes must be expressed in IaC, peer-reviewed, and testable in a staging account.
- Backward compatibility and graceful degradation: APIs and model rollouts should support compatibility guarantees and fallbacks.
- Cost-aware: design decisions should include estimated unit economics (tokens per second, GPU-hours, and expected cost per 1M tokens).

1) API Standards

Purpose: Ensure consistent, stable, and developer-friendly APIs across the platform (hosted API, dedicated, private).

1.1 URL and Resource Naming

- Use kebab-case for paths: /v1/inference, /v1/models/{model-id}/versions/{version-id}/predict.
- Versioning: include major version in the URL (v1, v2). Minor changes use header-based negotiation (Accept-Version) or model-version query params.
- Resource hierarchy: Keep resources noun-oriented (models, deployments, routes, keys). Avoid verbs in URIs.

1.2 HTTP semantics and gRPC

- Prefer REST+JSON for public-facing control-plane APIs and SDKs. gRPC is allowed for high-throughput internal connections between services (e.g., runtime <-> scheduler).
- Use appropriate HTTP status codes. For example: 200 for success, 202 for accepted async jobs, 400 for client errors, 401/403 for auth, 404 for unknown resources, 429 for rate limiting, 500/502/503/504 for server-side issues.

1.3 Request/Response shape and schema stability

- Use explicit top-level fields rather than deeply nested blobs. Example: {"request_id":"...", "model":"gptx-7b-q4", "input":"...", "response":{...}}.
- Schema evolution: Additive changes are allowed. Breaking changes must follow ADR and a deprecation plan with 90-day minimum for public APIs.

1.4 Error handling and observability

- Return structured errors: {"code":"model_not_ready", "message":"Model is warming up", "request_id":"...", "retry_after":30}.
- Log all 5xx responses with request_id, model, route, and span ids. 4xx errors should be logged at INFO with sample rate 0.01.

1.5 Rate limiting, quotas and throttling

- Apply per-api-key token-based quotas. Default burst limits: 100 qps for trial keys, configurable for enterprise.
- Use Retry-After header for 429 responses. Clients should implement exponential backoff with jitter.

1.6 Streaming and chunking

- Streamed responses must include delta messages with sequence ids and a terminal event. Include content-type: text/event-stream for SSE-like streaming or gRPC streaming for binary streams.

1.7 Authentication and authorization

- Auth: bearer tokens (short-lived) issued by control plane. Support mTLS for private deployment control channels.
- RBAC: map keys to project and team scopes; admin/checks must verify permission before destructive operations.

2) Coding Standards

Purpose: Maintain readable, testable, and secure code across services.

2.1 Languages and runtime choices

- Primary backend languages: Go (services, schedulers), Python (model adapters, evals), Rust/C++ (performance-critical runtime components). Use the language that best fits latency/throughput and operability needs.

2.2 Repos and modularity

- Prefer small, focused services with clear API boundaries. Shared libraries for common cross-cutting concerns (auth, metrics, tracing) must be versioned and published.

2.3 Code quality and reviews

- Mandatory PR review by at least one owner. Use CODEOWNERS for automatic reviewers. All PRs must pass linters and unit tests before merge.

2.4 Testing

- Unit tests: target 60% coverage for service code.
- Integration tests: every change touching infra or runtime should have an integration test in CI that runs in a sandbox account.
- E2E: critical user flows (model deploy -> infer) must have nightly E2E smoke tests with alerting on failures.

2.5 Static analysis and linters

- Use golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/mypy for Python, and clippy for Rust. Fail CI on new warnings for security-related linters.

2.6 Secrets and credentials

- No secrets in repo. Use secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) and reference via environment variables. All rotated keys must support automatic roll-forward.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, networking, capacity)

Purpose: Ensure consistent, secure, and reproducible infrastructure deployments.

3.1 IaC and environments

- Use Terraform for cloud infra (modules in org repo). Use Terragrunt where necessary for DRY patterns.
- Environments: dev (personal), staging (integration), prod. Changes must be promoted through these environments with automated plan/apply pipelines gated by approvals.

3.2 Networking and security

- VPC architecture: use isolated subnets per account, private-only control plane endpoints for Private deployments. 
- Use security groups and NACLs with least privilege. Harden control-plane endpoints: WAF in front of public APIs, private endpoints for admin consoles.

3.3 Image and packaging

- Container images must be built through CI, scanned for vulnerabilities (Snyk/Trivy), and signed. Base images should be pinned to digest.

3.4 Capacity and autoscaling

- Dedicated pools: reserve capacity in units of GPU-pools. Autoscaling policies must have cooldowns and max/min bounds.
- Capacity planning doc must include projected token/sec, 99th percentile request size, and expected concurrency per customer tier.

3.5 Backup and DR

- Critical state (metadata, audit logs) must be replicated across two regions with RPO < 15 minutes and RTO < 1 hour for control-plane functions.

4) Model-serving Standards

Purpose: Provide repeatable, observable, and performant model deployments across hosted, dedicated, and private modes.

4.1 Model packaging and artifacts

- Models must be versioned semantically (major.minor.patch) and accompanied by a manifest that lists: architecture, tokenizer, weight-format, quantization profile, supported sequence lengths, and KV cache compatibility.
- Example manifest table (as text):

  | field | example | notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | architecture | gptx | family name |
  | tokenizer | bpe-v2 | tokenizer repo tag |
  | weight-format | safetensors | exact file name and digest |
  | quantization-profile | q4_0 | reference to /confluence/quantization-profiles |

4.2 Quantization and perf profiles

- Quantization profiles must be in the central quantization-profiles directory and include tradeoffs (memory, throughput, accuracy delta). Each profile includes representative eval prompts and expected BLEU/ROUGE/LLM-eval deltas.

4.3 KV cache and prefix caching

- Runtime must document KV cache compatibility between versions. Prefix caching keys should be cache-key = sha256(model-id + prompt-hash + client-route). Cache TTL defaults: 24h for stable prompts, 5m for streaming ephemeral requests.

4.4 Rollouts, backwards compatibility and fallbacks

- Canary strategy: 5% -> 25% -> 100% over at least 30 minutes with automated health checks. Health checks include p50/p95 latency and error rate.
- Automatic fallback: if canary exceeds error budget or p95 latency doubles baseline, traffic should automatically shift to the previous stable variant.

4.5 Model validation and gating

- Before production rollout run: unit tests, perf bench (see section 6), and a quality evaluation against the model onboarding prompt set (pass threshold configurable per use-case).

4.6 Compatibility matrix

- Maintain a short compatibility matrix: runtime-version -> model-versions supported -> quantization profiles supported -> GPU kernel optimizations required. This file lives in eng-serving-runtime/runtime-compatibility and must be updated with each runtime release.

5) Observability Standards

Purpose: Make debugging and reliability engineering fast and unified across services.

5.1 Metrics

- Metric namespaces: redwood.<service>.<metric>. Use Prometheus exposition format for internal services.
- Required metrics on inference routes:
  - redwood.inference.requests_total (labels: model, route, status_code)
  - redwood.inference.latency_ms (histogram: le buckets covering 1ms..30s)
  - redwood.inference.tokens_generated_total
  - redwood.inference.kv_cache_hit_ratio (gauge)

- Cardinality control: limit label values for model and route; use hashed identifiers for high-cardinality inputs.

5.2 Tracing

- Use OpenTelemetry for traces. Ensure inference path emits spans for: API gateway, auth check, router, scheduler, runtime(infer), and storage calls. Propagate trace-id in response headers (X-Trace-Id).

5.3 Logs

- Structured JSON logs with these minimum fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, message, model, route, extra (free-form). Use sampling for verbose debug logs.

5.4 Dashboards and runbooks

- Every service must ship a default dashboard (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rates, QPS, token/sec) and an incident runbook that lists owners, mitigation steps, rollback steps, and postmortem checklist. Dashboards live in eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts.

5.5 SLOs and alerting

- Default SLOs for inference-hosted routes (per-tenant):
  - Availability: 99.9% (monthly)
  - Latency: p95 < 500ms for short completions (<=128 tokens), p95 < 1500ms for long completions (>512 tokens).
  - Error budget burn alert when 3-day burn rate > 5%.

- Alerting: use paging alerts for oncall when error-rate > 0.5% for 5m sustained on production routes or p95 latency increases by >2x from baseline.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarking

Purpose: Provide reproducible benchmarks and acceptable performance targets for model inference and runtime components.

6.1 Bench definitions

- Bench types: microbench (kernel-level), model-throughput (tokens/sec), end-to-end (API latency under realistic clients). Include dataset and prompt distributions used.

6.2 Benchmark lab and reproducibility

- Use the benchmarking-and-perf-suite repo. Bench runs must record hardware (GPU model, driver, CUDA/cuDNN/ROCm versions), environment (container image digest), model flavor (float16, q8, etc.), and full logs.

6.3 Target numbers (guidelines)

- For medium models (~7B, q4_0 on A100): expected throughput 1500 tokens/sec single-model on a single GPU in optimized runtime. These numbers vary by workload; always include median and 95% ranges.

6.4 Regression testing

- Performance regression tests run on every release candidate. Any release that regresses median throughput by >10% or increases p95 latency by >20% must include a mitigation plan in the release notes and an ADR if root cause requires design change.

7) Decision Records (ADR) Process

Purpose: Record architectural decisions with context, alternatives, and owners. ADRs make future reviews and rollbacks possible.

7.1 When to write an ADR

- ADR is required for any decision that affects cross-team APIs, infra topology, model-serving architecture, or SLO guarantees. Examples: switching RPC framework, changing cache topology for KV, changing default SLOs.

7.2 ADR template (single-file fields)

- Title (single line)
- Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
- Context (concise explanation of problem)
- Decision (what was chosen)
- Consequences (operational, cost, compatibility)
- Alternatives considered
- Owners (team and individuals)
- Date

7.3 ADR lifecycle and review

- Draft ADRs must be reviewed by owners of impacted areas and at least one member of eng-architecture. For public-facing changes, include product and go-to-market reviewers.

7.4 ADR metadata and index

- Each ADR must include: numeric id (YYYY-NNN), status, created_at, authors, and related_pages. An index page must list ADRs and their status; maintain in architecture-and-standards/decision-records-index.

Revision history

How to use this doc

- Link to this page from new project PRs that change API shapes, infra topology, or model-serving behavior. When in doubt, open an ADR.

Examples and snippets

- Example error response (JSON):

  {
    "code": "model_not_ready",
    "message": "Model is warming up - expected ready in 30s",
    "request_id": "req_123456",
    "retry_after": 30
  }

- Example Terraform requirement snippet (text):

  module "vpc" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-modules//vpc?ref=v1.4.0"
    env = var.env
  }

Contact and escalation

- For standard architecture questions open an issue in the architecture repo and tag eng-architecture. For incidents that touch model-serving, follow the runbook in confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks and page oncall via the pager duty alias.

End of document
